title: How wrong is the DC approximation of optimal power flow on the IEEE 30-, 39- and 118-bus cases?
lede: DC against AC optimal power flow in pandapower on the IEEE 30-, 39- and 118-bus cases: the DC model's cost is 1 to 3 % below the AC optimum (it ignores losses); on the 118-bus case its dispatch is feasible but costs 0.7 to 1.7 % more than the AC optimum once losses are paid, and on the 39-bus case it breaks voltage limits (15 buses at 0.6 of load) at almost no cost difference (modelled benchmark, not a measured system; tightened-limit runs often had no solution). Feeding the AC losses back into the DC model (a loss-adjusted DC) brings the 118-bus cost estimate to within 0.6 to 1.2 % of the AC optimum, but repairs only 13 to 32 % of the dispatch's excess cost and none of case39's voltage violations. On 23 PGLib-OPF benchmark cases with their published ratings (solver within 0.004 % of the library's optima), the DC dispatch overloads branches on all 11 congested (API) cases (worst 103 to 180 % of rating) and derating or iterated AC correction repairs only 1 of 11; MATPOWER's and PowerModels' DC OPFs differ by up to 2.8 %; successive linearisation of the AC power flow (loss factors and flow sensitivities from AC power flows, a QP, a step box) clears 7 of those 11 at the AC optimum's cost and leaves the rest within 0.012 % of their ratings. On PGLib's 12 angle-limited SAD cases, held out from that tuning, the same rules with linearised angle rows clear 7 of the 11 with an AC optimum at its cost (the angle-blind version 3). Without the oracle voltage schedule (case-file 1.0 pu setpoints), the same repair clears 2 of 11 congested and 2 of 11 angle-limited cases (6 and 7 with it), and a reactive stage after it is fully clean on 16 of 34 cases at a mean 0.8 to 4.3 % above the optimum's cost.
summary: The DC optimal power flow is the workhorse of dispatch and price studies; how much does it lose against the AC OPF? On pandapower's MATPOWER cases with their own quadratic costs, load scaled 0.6 to 1.1, both OPFs are solved and the DC set-points are run through an AC power flow (slack pays the losses). IEEE 118-bus (no branch limit binds): DC cost is 1.9–2.9 % below the AC optimum and its dispatch costs 0.7–1.7 % above it, with no violations. IEEE 39-bus: DC cost 1.0–1.5 % below, dispatch within 0.06 % of the optimum but 15, 5 and 1 buses out of voltage limits at 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 of load. IEEE 30-bus: DC 1.3–2.3 % below; at full load the DC dispatch overloads a branch to 111 % and is 0.31 % cheaper than the AC optimum, i.e. a violated constraint. Checks: a two-bus closed form and agreement of the cost function with pandapower. Limits: tightened-limit sweeps frequently returned no solution from the solver and non-convergence is not separated from infeasibility; 118-bus branch limits never bind so it is a losses-only comparison; no prices (LMPs), unit commitment or N-1; costs are the cases' own, not market prices. Modelled benchmark cases, not measured systems. Loss-adjusted DC (AC losses spread uniformly over loads, iterated 2–4 passes): the 118-bus cost estimate falls within 0.6–1.2 % of the AC optimum, but the AC cost of its dispatch is still 0.58–1.18 % above it (13–32 % of plain DC's excess recovered) and case39's voltage violations are unchanged; a uniform loss share fixes the price level, not the merit order. PGLib-OPF v23.07 with published ratings (2026-11-11): AC optima within 0.004 % of the library's IPOPT values on 23 of 24 cases; the published DC values are reproduced only with PowerModels' susceptance convention (MATPOWER's differs by up to 2.8 %). On the 11 congested (API) cases the DC cost is a median 6.5 % below the AC optimum, its dispatch overloads branches in every case (worst 103–180 %), it binds a median 56 % of the AC binding lines and its LMPs correlate at a median r = 0.66; uniform derating and an iterated loss-and-flow correction each clear the overloads on 1 of 11 API cases (8 typical cases clean). One AC solver, voltages held at the AC optimum's schedule, benchmark cases. Line outages (2026-11-11): penalty factors from the intact network's AC optimum, applied to the DC OPF after a single line trip on case118, beat plain DC on all 80 trips tested (loads 1.0 and 1.1; 0.409 against 1.671 % excess cost on the 20 most-loaded trips at load 1.0, oracle 0.367 %), keep at least 88 % of the post-trip oracle's gain, and lose most on the heaviest lines; case118's ratings do not bind, so a congesting trip is untested. AC-informed linearisation (2026-11-12): finite-difference loss factors and apparent-flow sensitivities from PYPOWER's AC power flow, a QP on the cases' costs. One linearisation at the plain DC dispatch clears 0 of the 11 API cases with an AC optimum; one at the AC optimum (oracle) clears 7; successive linearisation with a step box and an elastic l1 QP clears 7 within 10 rounds at the AC optimum's cost (within 0.001 %) and leaves the other four within 0.012 % of their ratings. Its step rules were tuned on the same cases (no held-out set); voltages held at the AC optimum's schedule; 1 to 13 s per case. Held-out test (2026-11-12): on PGLib's SAD cases (every branch angle limited to 4.7–16.2°; AC optima within 0.005 % of the published values on 11 of 12), the angle-blind method breaks up to 16 angle limits and lands 6.5–17.6 % below the optimum's cost; adding two linearised angle rows per branch, with the step rules unchanged, gives a dispatch clean on thermal, slack and angle limits on 7 of 11 at the AC optimum's cost, the tuning set's rate, and the misses end within 0.01 % of a limit. Voltage schedule (2026-11-12): at PGLib's own 1.0 pu generator setpoints instead of the AC optimum's, the angle-aware repair is clean on thermal, slack and angle limits on 8 of 12 TYP, 2 of 11 API and 2 of 11 SAD cases (oracle schedule: 7, 6, 7), and none of those dispatches meets voltage and Q limits; an AC OPF over voltages only, with P pinned, makes 16 of 34 fully feasible at a mean 0.8–4.3 % above the optimum's cost (worst 10.1 %), against 4 of 34 without the repair. Part of the programme grid-linopf.
